sentence: Abstract The companion paper models the Socratic-Platonic-Aristotelian corpus as a heteronymic configuration distributed across three functional positions: Socrates the orthonym, Plato the survival-heteronym, Aristotle the systematizing-heteronym.

title: Beautiful and New: The Second Letter's Socrates and the Editing of a Received Character (v0.2)
sentence: The *Second Letter* ends its most quoted sentence with a description no one takes at its verbs: there is no writing of Plato and never will be, and the things now said belong to a Socrates *become beautiful and new* — Σωκράτους ἐστὶν καλοῦ καὶ νέου γεγονότος.

title: Beautiful and New: The Second Letter's Socrates and the Editing of a Received Character (v0.2)
sentence: I argue that it describes an operation, not an attitude; that the operation is an edition — the revamping and inhabiting of a received character; that the base of the edition is a circulating character whose named, quoted, surviving instance the corpus itself cites — the *Apology*'s Aristophanic Socrates, received ἐκ παίδων; that the corpus performs the revision item by item, stripping the received figure of pay, teaching, and meteorology while cutting, again and again, the one boundary the base text had fused; and that the two adjectives of the letter name the two repairs that remained — καλός the inversion that keeps the ugly shell, νέος the reissue, its access to a young Socrates constructed through the corpus's longest chain of narrated transmission.

sentence: Plato idealized his teacher: the historical Socrates, old and famously ugly, appears in the dialogues transfigured — wiser, lovelier, more youthful than life; the letter, authentic or not, is the earliest witness to the gap between the man and the literary figure, and "beautiful and young" is its charming name for that gap.

sentence: Its subject is not a treatment of a person but the provenance of sayings: τὰ νῦν λεγόμενα, *the things now said*, are — the genitive is a genitive of author — *of Socrates*: and the Socrates they are of is specified by a perfect participle, γεγονότος — a Socrates *having become* beautiful and new.

title: Beautiful and New: The Second Letter's Socrates and the Editing of a Received Character (v0.2)
sentence: The base is not the historical Socrates, to whom the corpus's relation is beyond any text's reach; it is a *circulating* character — the work of πολλοὶ κατήγοροι over many years — whose named, quoted, surviving instance is Aristophanes' Socrates-the-sophist: the *Apology* names that instance, dates the reception, itemizes the received package, and quotes the play (§3).

sentence: And when the *Sophist* builds its taxonomy by division, the divisions land, six times, near enough that the sixth must be given its own flag: ἡ γένει γενναία σοφιστική, *the sophistry noble in lineage* (231b) — the refutative practice that looks, to every bystander, exactly like the thing being defined, and must be marked as its noble twin precisely because nothing but the mark separates them.[^5] A corpus that had received a Socrates-the-sophist and needed a Socrates-not-the-sophist would have to do exactly this: keep the practice, keep the look, and legislate the boundary again and again, because the boundary is the one item that cannot be inherited — it did not exist in the source.
